definition: Appeasement means the act of pacifying or satisfying someone by giving in to their demands, especially at the cost of one's own principles.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word appeasement. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know appeasement should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: At Munich in 1938, Britain's policy of appeasement handed territory to an aggressor in exchange for a promise of peace that lasted less than a year.
A compromise is a neutral trade where both sides give something up, while appeasement is lopsided — one side gives, hoping the other will simply stop demanding.
Capitulation is a complete surrender on every point, going beyond appeasement, which still imagines it is purchasing peace rather than admitting defeat.

Placation is the soothing of someone's anger in the moment — a free dessert, a quick apology. Appeasement goes further: it buys calm by surrendering one's own principles to the angry party's demands. You can placate without giving up anything that matters; appeasement always pays with principle.

Conciliation is a mutual effort to rebuild goodwill — both parties soften, both move toward the middle. Appeasement is one-sided: a single party gives and gives, hoping the demands will simply stop. Conciliation repairs a relationship between equals; appeasement feeds an appetite.

A concession is a single thing yielded in a negotiation, and trading concessions is how fair bargains get made. Appeasement is the whole strategy of yielding again and again while asking nothing back. One concession can be wise; a policy of appeasement only teaches the other side to demand more.
Defiance openly refuses the demands that appeasement would satisfy.
Resistance pushes back against pressure instead of buying peace by giving in.
The ambassador's pacific tone steered the tense meeting back to business within minutes.

The manager's appeasement of his rudest client — waiving fees and bumping her to the front of every queue — only taught her that complaining loudly always worked.
The sentence shows appeasement's core bargain: the manager buys temporary calm by surrendering fair rules, sacrificing principle to satisfy someone's demands.
formal / historical-political
Appeasement is almost always disapproving: it implies buying calm by sacrificing principle, and in historical writing it points specifically at the failed 1930s policy toward Nazi Germany.
Don't use it for an ordinary fair compromise — a compromise trades; appeasement surrenders.

When the magazine's star columnist threatened to quit unless editors stopped touching his late drafts, the editor gave way.
The next month he demanded approval of every headline, then a veto over the letters page; each time, the editor chose appeasement over confrontation, telling herself the demands would end.
Staff writers watched the standards they had been held to dissolve, one surrender at a time.
When the columnist finally insisted that a critical review of his friend's book be killed, the editor saw what the calm had been costing: the magazine's principles, paid out in installments.
She refused at last — and understood that every earlier surrender had only taught him to ask for more.
